item.title: Sleep and Nutrition: Foods That Could Help You Sleep Better
item.description:
Sleep

Sleep and Nutrition: Foods That Could Help You Sleep Better

Some foods can activate brain systems to aid falling asleep.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • The longer you are alive, the worse sleep typically becomes.
  • There is good scientific evidence to support certain nutrients as aids in falling asleep.
  • Tryptophan, bananas, beet juice, Magnolia bark, melatonin, lemon balm, and milk are just a few possibilities.

Millions of people around the world have poor sleep quality. If you’re reading this post, you’re likely one of those people. Sleep quality declines with normal aging. It’s inevitable. If your 10th birthday is a vague memory, then you’re probably not sleeping too well today. Humans sleep most soundly and deeply around the time of puberty. After those wonderful few years, sleep begins to degrade. The longer you are alive, the worse sleep usually becomes.

We cannot make our brain younger, but we can eat certain foods to counter the impact of poor sleep quality. The relationship between sleep and nutrition is not well studied. However, there is good scientific evidence to support these nutrients as aids in falling asleep.

Tryptophan‑Rich Foods

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that is a precursor to serotonin and melatonin, both of which positively influence sleep. Tryptophan can cross the blood-brain barrier, but not easily. Tryptophan must compete with virtually all of the other amino acids in the blood to get access to the brain. The best approach is to consume tryptophan-rich foods with a simple carbohydrate. The carbohydrate will induce insulin release, which will increase the percentage of tryptophan molecules that get across the blood-brain barrier.

A single dose of tryptophan (dietary or pharmaceutical) up to one gram will significantly reduce the time it takes to fall asleep without affecting sleep stages. This matters because most over-the-counter and medical prescriptions produce abnormal sleep patterns. Interestingly, tryptophan has minimal effects on healthy adults who fall asleep easily. Caution is necessary with supplements; too much pharmaceutical-grade tryptophan can produce eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, which can be fatal.

Bananas are high in magnesium, potassium, and tryptophan, which relax muscles and support the conversion of tryptophan into melatonin, aiding sleep onset. Almonds, walnuts, and pistachios are also rich in magnesium and melatonin. A small handful before bed can promote deeper, more restorative sleep.

The milk protein α-lactalbumin has the highest natural levels of tryptophan amongst all protein food sources. Other sources of tryptophan include chicken, fish, eggs, pumpkin seeds, beans, peanuts, cheese, and leafy green vegetables.

Melatonin

Naturally produced by the pineal gland, melatonin can also be taken as a supplement. Melatonin easily crosses the blood-brain barrier. A small dose 30 minutes to one hour before bedtime can help you feel sleepy more reliably. A placebo-controlled double-blind study on older adults who consumed a supplement containing 5 mg melatonin, 225 mg magnesium, and 11.25 mg zinc significantly improved subjective measures of sleep and total sleep time. The effects were attributed to the crucial roles both magnesium and zinc have in endogenous melatonin production. Melatonin is quite effective for reducing the symptoms of jet lag, but only when you’re traveling east.

Dosage is critical with melatonin. Begin with the lowest dose you can buy and break that pill into two pieces. Unfortunately, over the next few weeks, you will experience tolerance and higher doses of melatonin will be necessary. No more than 3 mg is advisable for sleep regularity. After a few months, you may need to take 10 mg to obtain any benefits. At that dose you may also experience daytime grogginess, headache, dizziness and a depressed mood. At higher doses you will likely experience vivid dreams and nightmares. If you find that you need higher doses of melatonin to get restful sleep, stop taking it for at least one month to allow your liver to recover and the neurobiological tolerance to dissipate. Finally, according to the American Heart Association, taking melatonin for more than one year significantly increased the risk of developing congestive heart failure.

You might also try tart cherries. Tart cherries contain high concentrations of melatonin. Studies have shown that consumption of tart cherry juice significantly reduced insomnia severity index scores and reduced the amount of time spent awake after sleep onset. You also stay asleep longer after falling asleep.

Beetroot Juice

The effect of 100 ml of beetroot juice on sleep has recently been reported (Bock et al., 2025). Subjective sleep quality improved significantly using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, which measures subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleep medication, and daytime dysfunction. The key ingredient in the beetroot juice that produced this effect was determined to be nitrate. Beet juice contains amino acids arginine and citrulline which are converted by the body into nitrates. The study found that a single pre‑sleep dose of inorganic nitrate (via beetroot juice, ~6.45 mmol) increased total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and slow‑wave sleep compared with placebo, and reduced wake after sleep onset. These effects were measured via polysomnography in healthy adults, and participants also reported better subjective sleep quality. A study in people with COPD (Alasmari et al., 2024) found that nitrate‑rich beetroot juice before bed reduced “disordered” sleep transitions and increased REM sleep in the last two hours of the night.

Magnolia Bark

Primarily extracted from the bark and seed cones of Magnolia officinalis, magnolia bark contains two relevant organic compounds, magnolol and honokiol. These compounds readily cross the blood-brain barrier and directly activate the GABA receptors in the brain. Their action is very similar to that of the widely used benzodiazepine drugs, such as Valium and Librium. Through this mechanism, extracts from magnolia bark enhance the calming effects of our own natural GABA production and keep the mind more at peace throughout the night, improving sleep quality and limiting interruptions. A 24-week study in menopausal women using a supplement containing 60 mg magnolia bark extract and 50 mg magnesium daily reported improvements in insomnia, anxiety, mood, and irritability.

Lemon Balm

Often used in sleep-inducing tea blends, lemon balm contains natural compounds that prolong the action of GABA. Higher levels of GABA reduce neural activity, allowing the mind to relax for a full night of restful sleep. Lemon balm and magnolia bark act on different steps of the GABA pathway—one preserves GABA availability, the other boosts receptor sensitivity—producing a synergistic calming effect without competing for the same metabolic pathways. Lemon balm is generally well tolerated, but several groups of people, anyone taking sedative medications, people with glaucoma, and those preparing for surgery should avoid it or use it cautiously.

Be aware that these foods will not reproduce the effectiveness of prescription or over-the-counter sleep medicines. The effects of these foods on the brain are more subtle.

item.title: The Strange Job of Being Our Brain's CEO
item.description:
Attention

The Strange Job of Being Our Brain's CEO

Why being in charge doesn’t mean being in control.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • Like a large organization, the brain does enormous amounts of work outside our conscious awareness.
  • Conflict and contradiction may simply be what it feels like to be a complex biological system.
  • We cannot micromanage our brain, but we can direct our attention, set priorities, and steer the ship.

What did you want to be when you grew up?

This is a pretty innocent question that all children are asked, and ask themselves. Mine was a baker, florist, musical instrument maker, and a U.N. worker at different times.

So when my friend said, “I want to be a CEO of a big company,” I was surprised. While it was probably just youthful blabber, I remember that comment vividly to this day.

The surprise was manyfold. I had no idea how one would become a CEO, or what that path would look like. But mainly, the surprise was because I myself would never want to be a CEO, even if (like a bad sitcom plot) somebody handed me that job.

Why this aversion?

It is not hard work I fear. What first comes to mind is a complicated organizational chart.

Messy organizational chart may resemble neurons?
Source: thomas-bethge/iStock

The many lines and arrows give me a headache because they symbolize this fact: the CEO is too far from, and cannot know, what is happening on the ground. The CEO reads the report without knowing exactly how it was made. Perhaps, intrinsically, I fear the lack of control, of not knowing everything that is happening.

The similarity between the brain and the corporate world

However, as much as I don’t desire to be a CEO of a human-made organization, this structure—a CEO having to be a leader without being able to know 100% of what is going on at the ground level—resembles something I am deeply familiar with: the workings of our brain.

Even though the brain is one of our organs, and we possess it and use it every day, we actually are not able to perceive the inner workings of our brain at the biological, neuronal level. We equate our brain with our self and mind, and feel emotions ranging from happiness to sadness and anger, use language, and form memories every day. But at any given moment, the brain is like a lively factory, humming and buzzing with an enormous amount of subconscious processing: sensory integration, autonomic regulation of bodily functions, memory retrieval, prediction, valuation, motor preparation and more. Conscious experience is only what surfaces and requires our attention: like an executive summary, not the underlying spreadsheet.

In this way, we are all CEOs of our own brain.

And this fits with modern theories of attention and consciousness. Experiments show that enormous amounts of neural processing occur outside conscious awareness. Philosopher Thomas Metzinger takes this idea further: the brain constructs a model of ourselves and the world, but we experience the contents of that model—not the machinery that constructed it. Most neural processing stays within specialized departments. Only some information makes it to the executive meeting.

A good CEO does not need nor will be able to know every single detail of the operation. Delegation allows the CEO to expend energy steering the ship without micromanaging every single detail.

Decision-making through complex bottom-up information

In a complex organization, there are many departments with competing agendas. Finance may be trying to tighten the belt while research and development may be embarking on a long-term project. The information coming up can be complicated and conflicting, and leaders need to make decisions factoring in competing interests.

Our brain is also incredibly complex, with different systems operating with different priorities. Basic instinctive survival needs, reward, habit, memory, social belonging, long-term planning, and prediction may point us in different directions. Simply deciding what to eat for lunch: a hamburger or salad? may involve competition among these different priorities.

In both corporations and our brains, contradiction and chaos are the norm.

Perhaps contradiction isn't evidence that we don't know ourselves. Contradiction may simply be what it feels like to be a complex biological system.

But who is the CEO?

In the end, this analogy only goes so far.

A CEO is an independent, separate person from the employees and the corporation; they can be removed or changed. But “we” cannot separate ourselves from our brain. It is not as if there is a small person sitting inside our head, ordering around all the other employee neurons.

So who is the “we” when I say “we” are the CEO of our brain?

The answer is: there is no single CEO sitting inside the brain.

Modern neuroscience tells us that conscious thoughts, attention, goals, and values themselves emerge from a distributed system. And yet, somehow, this system has the capacity to reflect upon itself, establish priorities, and influence what it does next.

Thus, maybe a better way to extend this analogy is this:

Let’s try to be a good CEO, using our attention and values like a mission statement, while understanding that we will never be able to perceive everything that is happening under our skull.

A bad CEO might try to micromanage every department, eliminate every disagreement, and demand that the organization behave exactly as intended. A good CEO knows that this is impossible. The organization is too large, too complicated, and filled with processes the CEO will never completely see.

What the CEO can do is set direction and steer the ship.

Our brains may require something similar from us. We cannot choose every thought that appears, every emotion that arises, or every impulse that asks for our attention. We cannot inspect the neurons that produced them. Sometimes we may not even understand why we want what we want.

But we can decide what deserves more weight. We can choose what we repeatedly attend to, what habits we cultivate, what environments we place ourselves in, and what values we return to when different parts of us pull in different directions.

Maybe that is the strange job each of us has been given: to steer an organization of astonishing complexity while seeing only a tiny fraction of what it is doing.

Thirty years later, I still don't want to be the CEO of a big company.

But apparently, I already have the job, and cannot escape it.
